dimensions.note: Comparative ethics sections 4 and 7: Tuan finds the brain-as-body/person distinction difficult and later avows her own decision in the confrontation with Miach. These are local tensions and represented commitments. Neither an integrated motivational hierarchy nor a stable general response policy follows from them; the analyst's defense of agency is not automatically Tuan's complete psychology.

The essay locates separate deliberative and final-confrontation moments, but a model of changes in Tuan's knowledge, commitments and dispositions between them has not been established. Mere narrative order does not supply a developmental transition rule.

The essay paraphrases first-person avowal and interprets its formal role. A source-language Tuan register, lexical repertoire, recipient-conditioned speech policy or acoustic voice has not been established from this evidence set.

The curated essay concerns political ethics and a final confrontation; a Tuan-specific account of ordinary routines or mundane responses has not been established. A description of the surrounding health society is not evidence of her every ordinary action.

Tuan's confrontation with Miach and response to Nuaza are identified, but a conditional account of how distinct relationships change her responses has not been established. The personally specific object of the final violence does not itself establish a relationship model.

Section 4 attributes difficulty defending a person/body boundary to Tuan; section 7 interprets her first-person avowal. This supports bounded questions about represented uncertainty and asserted agency. Avowal does not establish freedom from prior influence, all private motives, or the truth of every self-description.

Section 7, linked HAR-U019: Tuan avows a decision and directs final violence toward Miach. The essay distinguishes its personally specific object and bodily immediacy from Clavis's population-scale intervention. This constrains interpretation of that confrontation, not the frequency, escalation or resolution of other conflicts.

Sections 4 and 7 distinguish Tuan's difficulty with the treatment/personhood boundary, her asserted conscious choice, and the absence of moral vindication for revenge. These local deliberative tensions are supported; the comparative essay's broader normative argument is not a demonstrated Tuan decision procedure for unfamiliar ethical choices.
No Tuan-specific humor or play repertoire has been established from the curated comparative essay. This gap does not demonstrate an absence of humor in the character.

The complete active_provisional comparative essay was reviewed as repository analysis. Its Tuan discussion is bounded chiefly to the HAR-U014 treatment/personhood exchange and HAR-U019 final avowal, not a complete character corpus, original-witness rereading, separate monograph, model or HAR-U020 epilogue assessment.

Sections 4 and 7 provide affirmative countercases to flattening Tuan into a fully settled defender of autonomy whose conscious choices are necessarily benign: the treatment/personhood distinction troubles her, and her final asserted choice includes personally directed violence. These are local constraints, not proof that every future choice is violent or that agency is absent.

Section 4 identifies the HAR-U014 exchange and section 7 the HAR-U019 confrontation. They remain distinct disclosed moments, with the assessment ending at the latter. Later epilogue facts, an exact calendar time and a continuous intervening knowledge state are not established by this bounded assessment.

scenario_readiness.note: No generation or evaluation of new Tuan dialogue has been established. English analytical paraphrase of first-person avowal is not demonstrated Japanese dialogue competence.

No counterfactual or materially unfamiliar scenario has been assessed with fixed chronology, interlocutor relationship and setting constraints. No cross-scenario transfer or globally reusable Tuan model is asserted.
No readiness assessment for an ordinary new social encounter has been established from these political and climactic passages; ordinary functioning is not denied.
The essay supports interpretation of bounded canonical ethical tensions. No new ethical-choice scenario, conditional response procedure or independent predictive test has been established.

No romantic or relationship-scenario readiness assessment has been established. The personally specific confrontation with Miach does not determine behavior in another relationship or romantic setting.
No professional-response scenario or occupational behavior model has been established from this curated essay. Project-wide model labels and roles described elsewhere are not inherited.

known_limits.statement: Section 7 distinguishes Tuan's avowal of a conscious act from moral justification of revenge. Her actually violent choice prevents an unqualified inference that asserted agency always entails benign or consent-respecting action.

Section 4 attributes difficulty defending the brain-as-body/person distinction to Tuan. A rigid, fully settled rule rejecting every treatment of psychological suffering would erase that represented difficulty.

Section 7 expressly distinguishes Tuan's personally specific violence from Clavis's nationwide act. Formal first-person parallels cannot transfer his motives, technology, knowledge or scale of action to her.

This assessment establishes no complete weighting of Tuan's private motives, freedom from earlier influence, continuous knowledge trajectory, exact calendar placement or later epilogue state. Missing support is not evidence that a motive or capacity is absent.

Only the subject's directly curated comparative essay qualifies here. Her separate monograph, models, validation trials and original Japanese source have not been independently assessed in this run. Ordinary behavior, source-language voice, relationship transfer, humor and novel-scenario readiness remain unestablished within this evidence boundary, irrespective of broader material elsewhere.
